issues.issue: "any material property or assets" sets no threshold, so the date on which an Additional Collateral Date arises cannot be fixed. The trigger is equally open in referring to "any additional Project Contracts or Offtake Contracts" without value limits.

The closing condition, "on the same terms as the required by the Loans", is ungrammatical and leaves unclear what the Upstream Supplier Financing Creditors must require before the denominator includes their debt. The whole quotient therefore may or may not include items (ii) and (iii).

The definition closes each limb with "in each case to the extent arising in connection with the Additional Obligations", defining the term by reference to itself. The circularity leaves the boundary of the secured Additional Obligations indeterminate.

The closing catch-all, "each other security agreement or other security instrument or document executed and delivered to the reasonable satisfaction of the Security Agent", has no limit and sits against the enumerated categories. Its reach beyond documents required under Section 5.14 is uncertain.

"Borrowing" is defined to include "an LC Exposure", equating a contingent letter-of-credit exposure with an advance of funds. That makes it uncertain whether provisions keyed to a "Borrowing" (minimum amounts, Borrowing Requests, Interest Periods) apply to LC Exposure.

Section 2.04 and Section 2.03(d) treat every Borrowing as a funded Term Loan requiring a Borrowing Request and a $10,000,000 minimum, which cannot be squared with LC Exposure being a "Borrowing". The two readings pull in opposite directions.

Clause (c)'s parenthetical "(other than pursuant to the Security Documents" is never closed, so it is unclear where the carve-out for Liens ends. "Acceptable to the Lenders" also supplies no standard for the banks at which Cash may be held.

The clause presupposes Sweep Dates falling within the First Sweep Period, but that period as defined runs from nine months after the Scheduled Commercial Operations Date (no later than 30 June 2013) to 1 April 2014 and may contain no full fiscal quarter. Whether any First Sweep Period Sweep Amount can ever accrue is therefore contestable.

The defined term "Second Sweep Period Sweep Amount" is attached to the DSCR figure in excess of 1.15 rather than, as in clause (i), to the aggregate amount the Lenders may receive. On its face the sweep amount is the ratio, not the payment, which is a mechanical error that changes the calculation.
Payment of the Sweep Amount out of the DSRA on any deficiency sits awkwardly with Section 5.15's requirement that the DSRA be maintained at the Required Amount. Which obligation yields is not stated.

Because the Scheduled Commercial Operations Date cannot be later than 30 June 2013, nine months later is at latest 30 March 2014, so the First Sweep Period may be as short as two days and contain no "full fiscal quarter" for a Sweep Date. That cannot be reconciled with the Sweep Date definition and the Cash Sweep Mechanism clause (i).

The term takes its content from Cash Sweep Mechanism clauses (i) and (ii), but clause (ii) labels the DSCR excess rather than the payable amount as the "Second Sweep Period Sweep Amount". The definition therefore inherits an inconsistent meaning between the two limbs.
"Each full fiscal quarter during the applicable Sweep Period" cannot be applied to the First Sweep Period, which as defined may last only days. The two definitions do not fit together.

The definition makes the Sweep Payment Date fall one Business Day after the quarter in which a Sweep Date occurs, so (per the worked example) each Sweep Payment Date is itself a Sweep Date. Whether a single date can serve both functions in successive quarters is left unresolved.

A third party may acquire "more than 49%" of the Borrower's Equity Interests before a Change in Control occurs, yet the Pledged Borrower LLC Interests definition and the LLC Pledge Agreement require the Parent to hold and pledge at least 51%. The two thresholds do not sit comfortably together.

"Collateral" is defined as whatever is "Collateral" under any Security Document, so its content is entirely delegated to documents outside this Agreement. The scope of the secured pool cannot be determined from the instrument itself.

The definition conditions the Commercial Operations Date on certification by the "Lenders' Engineering Consultant", a term the Agreement never defines; Section 1.01 defines only "Engineering Consultant". Whether the two are the same person is left to construction.

"Project financing lent to the Borrower by a Subsequent Project Lender ... and in which the Lenders under this Agreement become a party" states no mechanism or obligation, and "may be subject to an Intercreditor Agreement" is permissive. What, if anything, binds the existing Lenders is unclear.

The parenthetical carve-out in clause (b) disclaims all representations about data-room documents "unless the subject matter of such document is otherwise included in a representation or warranty set forth in Article III", leaving the residual scope of the disclaimer uncertain. The interaction of the disclaimer and Article III is the point of contest.

The proviso lets the Borrower and a counterparty substitute Minnesota or other governing law into the Consent and Agreement "without the consent of the Required Lenders or the Security Agent being required", with no limit on which laws qualify. What the Secured Parties have agreed to accept is therefore open-ended.

"The power to direct or cause the direction of the management or policies of a Person ... by contract or otherwise" has no percentage benchmark, so control is a matter of judgment in every case. The catch-all "or otherwise" widens it further.

After the specifics "cash, inventory and accounts receivable", the catch-all "other assets that are due, or likely to be converted into cash, sold, exchanged, or expensed in the normal course of business, within one (1) year" turns on the vague test "likely to be". Its reach against the enumerated items is genuinely uncertain.

"Any matters disclosed in the Confidential Information Material" incorporates an entire information memorandum and data site without identifying what counts as a disclosed matter. The breadth of the carve-out from representations is left at large.
"Any items treated as exceptional or extraordinary items" gives no standard for who so treats them or by what criteria. The add-back is therefore capable of materially different computations.

The Commercial Operations Date definition requires certification by the "Lenders' Engineering Consultant", a label that does not match this defined term. Whether Noramco acting under this definition is the same certifier is left open.

"Relating in any way to the environment" coupled with "notices or binding agreements" as sources of law makes the category of Environmental Laws very hard to bound. The width of "in any way" is the contestable point.

The catch-all "any other material contract entered into by the Borrower with respect to any engineering, procurement or construction services" follows four named contracts, and "material" is undefined. Whether a given supply or services contract is an EPC Contract is left to argument.

The Borrower must deposit "all Cash and receivables arising out of any contracts of the Borrower with any Person or payments otherwise received by Borrower", a sweep of literally every receipt with no carve-out for operating funds. How far that obligation actually reaches is a live question.

Everything deposited is said to be "applied in accordance with the Cash Sweep Mechanism", yet Section 2.05 requires Loans to be funded into the same Escrow Account and then "made available to the Borrower" for Project costs. The two directions for the same account cannot both be applied literally.

The definition ends by preserving "any successor collateral agent appointed pursuant to the Collateral Account Agreement", although the office being defined is escrow agent and account bank and the Agreement separately appoints a Security Agent. The mismatched label leaves the succession mechanism uncertain.

The definition omits the operative verb — "'Existing Credit Agreement' the Credit Agreement dated September 22, 2010" — so it is a sentence fragment. The omission is trivial to cure but is a mechanical defect on the face of the text.

The numerator is limited to assets over which the Secured Parties hold a first priority interest "subject only to Permitted Liens thereon", but the Agreement defines "Permitted Encumbrances", not "Permitted Liens". The undefined term makes the FACR calculation contestable.

Financial Closure requires Total Commitments of US$530,000,000, but the Total Commitment definition fixes US$250,000,000 unless Accession Agreements are entered into, and Section 2.02(b) makes Tranche B available only after Financial Closure. Whether Tranche B can ever be drawn absent accession is a genuine question.

The long enumerated list of events closes with "or other similar acts beyond the reasonable control of the Borrower", a classic ejusdem generis catch-all whose reach against the specifics is uncertain. "Similar" to which of acts of God, strikes, weather or machinery breakage is not stated.

"A jurisdiction other than that in which the Borrower is located" turns on the undefined notion of where a borrower is "located", and the final sentence contemplates a Borrower located in more than one jurisdiction. The test for Foreign Lender status is therefore not self-applying.

"And related proceedings thereto that may be filed elsewhere in Federal or state court" extends the defined litigation to unidentified future proceedings without any test of relatedness. What falls inside the Great Lakes Litigation, and hence inside the disclosed matters, is left open.

The parenthetical label is misplaced: "guaranteeing any Indebtedness (the \"primary obligor\")" attaches the defined label to the Indebtedness rather than to the obligor who owes it. The clauses that follow then use "primary obligor" as a person, which the definition does not supply.

"Other derivative transaction of any kind or nature" is a catch-all following three named categories with no limiting principle. Whether ordinary commercial supply arrangements fall inside it is arguable.

Clause (f) adds "any obligation undertaken by such Person in the nature of a payment obligation" after ten specific categories, a catch-all wide enough to swallow the enumeration. Its reach against the listed items is a classic ejusdem generis question.

The account is defined by reference to "clauses (i) through (vi) of Section 2.11(c)" and to allocation rules "set forth in the Collateral Account Agreement", so its operation depends wholly on documents and subclauses not reproduced here. Any mismatch between them and this definition would have to be construed.

Describing the Interest Election Request as "the one-time request ... with respect to the duration of Interest Periods" leaves unclear how, if at all, the Borrower may elect for later Borrowings. The single-election concept is stated only in the definition.

Limb (b) runs "(i) the first Interest Period ... and (iii) thereafter", omitting any clause (ii), and the proviso then re-uses the labels (a), (b) and (c) already used for the limbs. The numbering gap leaves it uncertain whether a provision was dropped.

Limb (b) promises "the sum of (i) ... plus the aggregate amount of all LC Disbursements", but no clause (ii) is ever given, so the second addend floats outside the enumeration. The construction of the Lender-level LC Exposure figure is thereby muddled.

The definition treats an assignee as one "that becomes a Project Lender", but the Recitals define "Project Lenders" to include providers of supplier's credit as well as term lenders. Read together, the class of persons who can be a "Lender" is inconsistent.

The closing condition "on the same terms as the required by the Loans" is ungrammatical, leaving unclear when items (ii) and (iii) enter the denominator and so what each Lender's share actually is. The pro rata percentage cannot be computed with confidence.

This definition keys off mandatory prepayments "in accordance with Section 2.11(b)", while the parallel Upstream Supplier Financing Creditor's and Additional Indebtedness Holder's Pro Rata Interest definitions key off Section 2.11(f). The differing cross-references make the sharing mechanics hard to reconcile.

The definition caps expiry at "four (4) years from the date of this Agreement" (29 December 2014) yet clause (4) allows negotiation of a letter of credit up to 30 December 2014. The two dates cannot both be given effect.

The primary source is the Reuters "LIBOR01" screen, while the Market Disruption Event definition triggers on the "LIBO01" screen rate and on quotations from Reference Banks that this definition does not use. The two rate-setting mechanisms are not aligned.

The list closes with "any other document designated from time to time as a Loan Document by the Lenders or the Facility Agent", a unilateral power to enlarge the category with no consent from or notice to the Borrower. How far that catch-all extends beyond the enumerated documents is a real question.

Clause (a) ends "shortfall undertakings or payment undertakings or any nature whatsoever, and other term liabilities", where "or any nature" should read "of any nature"; as written the phrase is a free-standing catch-all. Its reach against the enumerated debt categories is unclear.

Every limb turns on what "Required Lenders determine", including the wholly subjective judgment in (iii) that their cost of matching deposits "would be" above the LIBO Rate. Whether that determination is reviewable at all is left unsaid.

"Material adverse effect" on the Borrower's "business, financial condition, operations or performance or properties ... since March 31, 2010" states no threshold, duration or benchmark for materiality. MAE clauses of exactly this shape are standard fodder for construction disputes.

"All material approvals and consents by any Person" is defined by a schedule and then extended "including, but not limited to, environmental permits, rights for developing mines ... or a mining plan, if required". Whether an unlisted approval is "material" and so within the term is left open.

Limb (ii) brings in "any and all mining rights and leases of the Borrower with acknowledgment from the relevant Government Authorities or other Person which is a lessor consenting to such Mortgage", so whether a mining lease is Mortgaged Property depends on a third party's act. Until consent is given the status of the asset is indeterminate.

The arithmetic labels are broken: "(i) the sum of (A) ... minus, (B) ... and (C) minus mark-to-market amounts" makes (C) a subtraction inside a "sum", and the US$25,000,000 qualifier attaches ambiguously to individual or aggregate amounts. The computation of Net Debt is genuinely uncertain.

Each limb is qualified "in each case to the extent arising in connection with the Obligations", so the definition of Obligations is expressed by reference to itself. The circularity leaves the outer boundary of the secured debt open to argument.

"Obligor" is defined as "any of the Borrowers or any Guarantor", using a plural that the Agreement never defines — Section 1.01 defines a single "Borrower", Essar Steel Minnesota LLC. The mismatch leaves the class of Obligors imprecisely stated.

The carve-out for "any spot sale contract providing for payment within forty-five (45) days" is undefined as to what makes a sale a "spot" sale, and the sentence ends without a period. Whether a given sales contract is an Offtake Contract can turn on that label.

"De-bottlenecking and other similar performance and operational and efficiency enhancing modifications" is a general phrase resting on one example, with no test for what counts as efficiency enhancing. Whether particular capital expenditure qualifies for the US$50,000,000 basket is left at large.

The closing proviso says the term "shall not include any Lien securing Indebtedness on Attributable Debt", where "on" is plainly an error for "or"; as written the carve-out has no sensible referent. Since the proviso removes items from an eighteen-limb list, the mistake changes what is permitted.

The opening words require that the Borrower "has received the prior written consent of the Required Lenders" for the change, but the final proviso says that for de-bottlenecking modifications "the prior written consent of the Required Lenders shall not be required" if equity-funded. The definition thus both requires and dispenses with the same consent.

The sentence collapses: "includes any Permitted Project Change subject to the receipt of approval, if any, required in the definition of Permitted Project Change has been approved as set forth in the definition of that term". Whether an unapproved change is part of the Project cannot be read off the words.

Two nested provisos give "Project Contracts" different meanings for different purposes — excluding sub-threshold and Schedule 1.01E contracts for Consent and Agreement purposes while including only above-threshold contracts for Sections 6.09 and 6.10 — and clause (a) contracts are carved back in. Which meaning governs a given use is genuinely contestable.

The Recitals define "Project Lenders" to include providers of supplier's credit as well as the term lenders, yet the operative provisions (for example the definitions of Lender and Required Lenders) treat Project Lenders as Term Loan lenders only. The recital and the operative text point in different directions.

The definition points to a date "specified in the financial Covenants", but Section 6.12 (the defined Financial Covenants) is not shown to specify any "Relevant Date". If no such date is specified the definition is empty.

Two different periods are given — each fiscal year, and each rolling period from the start of the second half of one year to the end of the first half of the next — with no rule for which applies when. Both limbs are stated as "Relevant Period" without any "or" or ordering.

The date is to be "mutually determined by the Required Lenders and the Borrower at the time of Financial Closure", yet Financial Closure requires US$530,000,000 of commitments that may never arise, and the First Sweep Period is measured from this date. If Financial Closure never occurs the sweep machinery has no start point.

The definition promises a "first perfected security interest in the Collateral ... including all assets and properties of the Borrower" and then, in the same sentence, subordinates the Current Assets security to any Working Capital Bank Financing. The grant is therefore first priority and junior at once.

The FACR definition computes coverage from assets "over which the Secured Parties have a first priority security interest", which the Current Assets proviso here contradicts for that asset class. The two definitions cannot both be applied literally.

Clause (a) includes "deferred payment guaranties, shortfall undertakings or payment undertakings or any nature whatsoever", where "or any nature" is an error for "of any nature" and leaves a catch-all with no stated referent. Its reach against the enumerated items is unclear.

The definition joins a consolidation test and a fifty-percent voting test with "as well as", so it is unclear whether both or either suffices. The lower-case term is also only a hair's breadth from the separately defined "Subsidiary".

Supplier Financing is capped at US$183,000,000, while the Financial Closure definition requires Supplier Financing "made available" of US$182,750,000 and the Recitals speak of about US$713,000,000 of overall Project financing. The figures do not line up cleanly across the instrument.

The availability period ends 30 September 2013, yet Letters of Credit issued up to 30 June 2013 may run 36 months and their disbursements automatically convert into Term Loans under Section 2.06(e) long afterwards, even though Section 2.01 says undrawn Commitments lapse at the end of this period. The two cannot both operate literally.

The final sentence reads "shall be set forth or in the Assignment and Assumption or Accession Agreement", a stray "or" leaving the alternative sources of a Subsequent Project Lender's commitment garbled. It is not clear whether a third source was intended.

The Maturity Date is 1 January 2020, a day on which New York and Minnesota banks are closed and so not a Business Day, yet Section 2.09 both requires payment on "the next preceding Business Day" and requires the final installment to be paid "on the Term Loan Maturity Date". Those directions conflict for the last payment.

Clause (b) adds "Short-Term Debt and Working Capital Bank Finance" even though the Short-Term Debt definition subtracts working capital financing at its clause (d), so the same debt is deducted and added back, contrary to Section 1.03's direction that calculations "shall not include any double counting of items". The label "Working Capital Bank Finance" also does not match the defined term.

The definition tails off into narrative — "certain of which Unsecured Subordinated Promoter Loans are excluded from certain definitions as used herein" — without identifying which loans or which definitions. It also purports to summarise the Section 6.07 payment restriction rather than define a term.

The closing words "on the same terms as the required by the Loans" are ungrammatical, leaving unclear the condition on which items (ii) and (iii) enter the denominator. The creditor's share cannot be computed with confidence.

The section says undrawn Term Loan Commitments "lapse automatically at the end of the Term Loan Availability Period" and bars re-borrowing, yet Section 2.06(e) automatically converts LC Disbursements into Term Loans on letters of credit that may remain outstanding for 36 months from issuance. A conversion after 30 September 2013 cannot be squared with the lapse rule.

Tranche B becomes available only "on and after the Business Day on which Financial Closure shall occur", and Financial Closure requires aggregate Total Commitments of US$530,000,000 when the Total Commitment is US$250,000,000 absent Accession Agreements. Whether the US$100,000,000 Tranche B is ever drawable turns on reconciling those definitions.

"The payment of the Project's costs and Transaction Costs amounts" is garbled and "the Project's costs" is nowhere defined, so the permitted end use of proceeds has no fixed boundary. The Borrowing Request must state an "end use" measured against it.

The flat prohibition that "no proceeds shall be used to fund or maintain the DSRA" sits uneasily with Section 2.06(j), which requires the Borrower to pay cash collateral into the DSRA on an Event of Default. Whether borrowed funds may end up there is left unresolved.

"In not more than fifteen (15) Borrowings" does not say whether the cap is on Borrowings in the aggregate, per Lender or per tranche. The minimum-amount parenthetical adds a further alternative that is not tied to the count.

The sentence "shall notify the Facility Agent and the Escrow Agent and Account Bank of such request and in writing not later than 1:00 p.m." is garbled as to whether oral notice plus written confirmation, or a single written notice, is required. The five-Business-Day requirement is then waived for the first Borrowing without any substitute period.

Loans are to be funded into the Escrow Account and then "made available to the Borrower" for its stated purposes, while the Escrow Account definition says all amounts deposited there are "to be applied in accordance with the Cash Sweep Mechanism". The two treatments of the same account pull apart.

The paragraph limits letters of credit by reference to "the applicable limitations on the Initial Lender Tranche A Commitment set forth in Section 2.02(a)", but Section 1.01 defines only "Initial Lender Tranche A Total Commitment" and Section 2.02(a) sets sub-facility limits. The referenced limitation is not identified by any defined term.

The six documentary alternatives are joined by "or" and close with "(vi) such other documents as may be specified by the Issuing Bank from time to time", an open-ended addition to an enumerated list. What the Borrower must actually deliver is left in the Issuing Bank's hands.

This paragraph caps expiry at the earlier of 36 months from issuance and four years from the Agreement's date (29 December 2014), while the "Letter of Credit" definition permits negotiation up to 30 December 2014. The outer date differs by a day between the two provisions.

Automatic conversion of an LC Disbursement into a Term Loan takes no account of Section 2.01, under which undrawn Commitments lapse at the end of the Term Loan Availability Period and no Term Loan may exceed the Lender's Unused Commitment. A conversion after that date has no commitment to draw on.

The paragraph states the Issuing Banks have no liability "irrespective of ... any other event or circumstance whatsoever", then preserves liability for direct damages caused by a failure "to exercise care", and then deems care to have been exercised absent gross negligence, wilful misconduct or fraud. The exclusion and the carve-back set two different standards.

This paragraph gives the Issuing Bank "the final word" on document compliance and bars the Borrower from questioning it absent gross negligence, wilful misconduct or fraud, whereas Section 2.06(f) expressly preserves the Borrower's claim for direct damages caused by the Issuing Bank's failure to exercise care. The two standards of review conflict.

The cash collateral is paid into the DSRA even though Section 2.02(d) provides that no proceeds "shall be used to fund or maintain the DSRA", and the security interest is granted to "the Lenders" although all Collateral elsewhere is held by the Security Agent for the Secured Parties. Both points require reconciliation with those provisions.
The subsection enumerates "(i) the first Interest Period ... and (iii) thereafter", with no clause (ii) anywhere. The gap leaves it open whether a step in the election mechanics has been omitted.

The election is to be made "in its first Borrowing Request", yet Section 1.01 defines the Interest Election Request as a separate one-time request and Section 2.04 lists the Interest Period only as an item of the first Borrowing Request. Whether one document or two is required is not clear.

The first sentence permits cancellation "upon prior written notice" yet "immediately upon such notice", and the later sentence then says the Lender "shall endeavor to provide prior notice" except where creditworthiness has deteriorated. Whether prior notice is a condition or merely an endeavour is contradicted within the same paragraph.

The Borrower's right to reduce turns on whether "the Project costs shall have been reduced below one billion ninety seven million Dollars", but "Project costs" is nowhere defined and no measurement date or method is given. The trigger cannot be applied without construction.

The US$1,097,000,000 figure appears only in the Recitals as a current estimate of total Project cost, yet this operative provision uses it as a fixed benchmark. Recital and operative text therefore pull differently on what the number means.

Repayment is fixed by reference to "all Term Loans outstanding on the last day of the Term Loan Availability Period", yet Section 2.06(e) creates new Term Loans by automatic conversion of LC Disbursements after that date. The table of percentages says nothing about amortising those later Loans.
